newsitem.title: UK: French desperately need higher dlr/mark - analysts.
newsitem.headline: French desperately need higher dlr/mark - analysts.

text.p: The French government needs a higher dollar/mark rate to resolve economic problems highlighted in the big domestic debate about foreign exchange policy but it also needs the collusion of the Bundesbank to achieve it.

Increasingly vocal critics of French exchange rate policy believe the dollar is grossly undervalued against the German mark, the franc and other European currencies. This has slowed French growth and employment for years by giving U.S. exports a competitive edge, they argue.

The big problem for French policymakers is how to engineer or coax the dollar higher against the franc without appearing to adopt an independent devaluationist stance akin to the early 1980's, one which would destabilise the franc against the mark.
A blowout in the mark/franc rate could risk destroying the whole process toward European monetary union in 1999.

"There's desire in France to relate a large part of their competitive disadvantage to exchange rates but, crucially, they want to see European currencies as a whole weaker against the dollar, not a weaker franc against the mark," said Brian Hilliard, economist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull.
"Nevertheless, there is an inevitable rise in market tension about the whole franc fort policy as a result."

France's long-standing "franc fort,' or strong franc policy, centres on maintaining mark/franc's almost 10-year old central exchange rate in the European exchange rate mechanism. This policy has survived since January 1987 through socialist and conservative governments and currency crises in 1992 and 1993.

But the French franc was undermined across the board on Thursday against the dollar and the mark after comments from Bank of France member Jean-Pierre Gerard. He is one of three members of the central bank's nine-person policy-making council who are seen as sceptical about the wisdom of franc fort.

Centrally, Gerard argued for a higher dollar against the franc and the mark, calling for a dollar/franc rate as high as 6.00 and dollar/mark as high as 1.87 (compared with 5.2060 and 1.5330 today). But, he said that without a better Bundesbank understanding of the monetary policy impact of monetary union, the mark/franc link may have to be modified.

"Gerard is very much on the dovish extreme on the Bank of France but there's no doubt the steady stream of these comments does create creeping suspicions about franc fort," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economic adviser at Bank of America.

Gerard went on to advocate monetary easing in France independent of the Bundesbank, which he believes is unrealistically clinging to an overvalued mark at a dangerous time in German and European economies.

"Even if Germany still has its economic merits, its industrial fabric is eroding, it has a considerable level of unemployment, its labour costs are well above ours, work hours are shorter and its external trade balance is less favourable than in the past," said Gerard.
"They are clinging to the monetary policy of mark stability but I do not believe this is the reason for their past success. It is rather a result of it."
"The French are making play for a more politicised monetary regime in Europe and will try to bring Italy on board to provide more clout," said Roger Francis, economist at IBJ International.

Gerard's dollar and interest rate remarks echoed comments earlier in the week from fellow Bank of France council member Paul Marchelli. The currency debate was reopened on November 20 by former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing.

Since Giscard d'Estaing initial comments, dollar/franc has surged about three percent to a peak at 5.2100 Tuesday. Mark/french franc has also risen but by a fraction of the dollar move as dollar/mark also pushed higher and traders were wary of mark sales from the Bank of France above 3.3950 francs.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe remains resolute about existing policy but will surely be pushing for the dollar to the return to the agenda of the next meeting of the Group of Seven industrialised nations early next year.
